title: Community acceptance of aquaculture introduction varies across food, economic, and ecological goals
content:
Abstract

Aquaculture has been identified as a viable approach to address the socio-ecological challenges facing wild-capture fisheries. However, its success is not merely a technocratic matter of deploying new technology; it depends on communities' acceptance and active participation. This is especially important for communities deeply connected to wild-capture fisheries, where aquaculture may be perceived as disrupting their identity and well-being. Framing plays an important role in community acceptance, as the ways in which aquaculture's benefits are presented can shape levels of public support. We examined community acceptance of aquaculture by comparing framings around food security, environmental benefits, and economic development and by identifying the factors that shape support within each. Using a structured questionnaire administered to 948 North Carolina residents, we found that community acceptance differed significantly depending on how the benefits of aquaculture were framed. Support for aquaculture was highest when framed in terms of economic benefits and lowest when framed in terms of ecological benefits. The predictors of acceptance varied across framings. However, the perceived need for aquaculture was the only factor that consistently influenced support across all outcomes. These findings highlight that aquaculture's legitimacy and acceptance depend on the alignment between emphasized benefits and residents' individual values, climate attitudes, and perceived local priorities. More broadly, they suggest that communication strategies for aquaculture development may be more effective when tailored to the values and concerns most salient to the intended audience and that governance processes attentive to community expectations may help build broader support.
